1.why: All nine screenshots show a static, uncluttered card layout with no moving images, animations, or pop-ups.

2.why: Primary actions use high-contrast blue buttons and bold headings that clearly stand out from body text and secondary links.

3.why: Each screen is single-purpose with the main field and button immediately visible, though the overall multi-step flow still requires navigation.

4.why: The user must complete many sequential steps (email/token, recovery MFA, new password rules, sign-in MFA) and retain complex requirements.

5.why: No password-manager hints, autofill controls, or “remember me” options appear on any of the forms.

6.why: Aside from simulation pre-fills in the Logs panel, the interface shows no saved or familiar items the user can recognize.

7.why: Labels, instructions, and notices across all screens are short, plain-language sentences that are easy to read.

8.why: None of the nine screenshots display any error messages, so their helpfulness cannot be verified.

9.why: Step 1 gives an explicit contact example and the password screen lists character rules; other steps include brief usage notes.

10.why: Only password and six-digit code entry are offered; no alternative methods such as face login or choice among factors are presented.

11.why: Every screen limits the user to one primary action or a single binary checkbox, never a large set of simultaneous choices.

12.why: Screens explicitly confirm outcomes such as “recovery instructions have been prepared” and “Privacy statement accepted.”

13.why: Contextual tips appear (password composition rules, token lifetime, safe-authentication notices) on most steps.

14.why: Forms can be re-submitted, yet no explicit “try again,” edit, or back controls are visible in the screenshots.

15.why: Header, card layout, button styling, typography, and the green safe-auth notice remain identical across all nine steps.
